body:
Compressed materialization now resolves its casts through the database's `CastFunctionSet`, like every other cast. User-registered casts apply here too.

- `CreateStatsAwareCast` uses `AddCastToType`. `PropagateCastStatistics` and `ValuePreservingCastFits` use the registered cast set. If a registered cast cannot propagate statistics, the integral compression falls back to the dedicated compress functions.
- `CMUtils::MarkCast` no longer asserts a default cast.
- SQL export drops the compressed materialization cast and exports its child, so it no longer rejects a non-default one.
- Compression assumes casts are correct for in-range values. An incorrect registered cast can produce wrong results here, as it can anywhere else.

This replaces the built-in-only casts that duckdb/duckdb#28757 kept for compressed materialization (`CreateDefaultStatsAwareCast`).

comments.body:
Thanks. Both points come from the same underlying issue. Compressed materialization adds casts the query never asked for. Using registered casts there exposes cast-free queries to whatever a user-registered cast does, so this is not "as anywhere else", as the description claims. The endpoint round trip and the statistics callback do not show that a cast preserves values or order, as your 0..100 example shows.

I see three options:

1. Keep CM on built-in casts only, i.e. the base's fresh built-in `CastFunctionSet` from #28757, and close this PR. CM is an internal rewrite, so the user's casts arguably should not apply to it.
2. Use a registered cast only if it declares itself value- and order-preserving (an explicit flag on the cast function) and has a statistics callback. Otherwise use the built-in cast. The probe would also have to run only after these eligibility checks and treat any exception as "not usable", not only `ConversionException`. That is your second point.
3. Keep the current behaviour and document the risk. I don't recommend this.

I would go with 1, or 2 if registered casts in CM are actually needed. @Mytherin @kryonix, which do you prefer? I'll update the PR or close it accordingly.

I dont really see why sqlexport needs to differentiate between built-in and non-default casts at all. 

Yes, you may end up with differing semantics/result if you export and re-execute a sql fragment where the casts have been overridden on either side, but thats also true for e.g. extension functions that REPLACE_ON_CONFLICT, settings, etc. I don't think its worthwhile trying to protect against this for just casts as there is so much other stuff that will be environment/config/extensions-loaded sensitive during both binding and execution anyway.

Agreed. This PR only removed the compressed-materialization case. The remaining distinction comes from two checks in `ExportCast` that predate it:

- `default_cast_binding` rejects exporting a default-bound cast when a registered cast could override that conversion.
- The aggregate-state branch rejects a cast when a registered cast could override either the state type or its storage type.

As far as I can tell, they protect only the plan-verification round-trip: a test that registers a cast overriding a built-in would re-bind the exported SQL to the override and mismatch. That is the same environment sensitivity you describe for `REPLACE_ON_CONFLICT` functions and settings, and we don't guard those. So I'd drop both checks and export casts as plain `CAST`/`TRY_CAST` regardless of where they came from. The aggregate-state check would keep its `TRY_CAST` rejection, which is about representability. Any test that deliberately overrides a built-in cast can opt out of the verification instead.

Happy to open that as a follow-up PR. CC @kryonix since these came from the SQL-export work: is there a case I'm missing where the default/registered distinction matters beyond verification?

review_comments.body:
This endpoint check can fail a cast-free query even when CM would reject the cast. It executes registered casts during planning, before checking eligibility or requiring a statistics callback; the guard catches only `ConversionException`.

With registered BIGINT-to-TINYINT/UTINYINT casts that have no statistics callback and throw `InvalidInputException`, the same BIGINT 0..100 table gives:

```sql
SELECT list(i)[49:53] FROM (SELECT i FROM t ORDER BY i);
```

CM on fails with “Invalid Input Error: registered cast called”; disabled returns [48, 49, 50, 51, 52]. Decide eligibility before executing registered casts. Keeping the built-in casts would also avoid this failure.

title: Let compressed materialization use registered casts
